title: Photo-Cartoon Object Companion 01
prompt:
Turn each portrait photo I upload into its own premium design poster. Output one image per photo — no multi-image collages.

Use a 3:4 vertical layout with a clear top/bottom split. Keep both zones roughly balanced in height, but never stretch or distort the original photo to force a ratio. Keep a clean, sharp horizontal boundary between the zones.

Top half: faithfully preserve the original photograph — identity, facial features, expression, hairstyle, pose, clothing, gestures, real objects, spatial relationships, natural lighting, and original color mood. Only apply slight premium photo grading and ultra-fine film grain. Do not redraw the person or change their identity.

Bottom half: place the same person as a high-fidelity photographic cutout on a simple solid-color field. The person must stay photoreal — never turn them into illustration or a cartoon character.

From the original photo, pick one real object already present and most closely related to the person (camera, drink cup, suitcase, fruit, book, or personal item) and turn it into the single personified cartoon companion. Keep the object's real shape, color, and recognizable features; add thick black rubber-hose limbs, oval eyes, white gloves, light halftone dots, and restrained retro animation print texture.

The cartoon object must not just sit beside the person — it needs clear spatial interaction (holding hands, handing something, cheers, hug, reacting, or walking together). Interaction should feel natural, playful, and instantly readable. Do not cover the face. Do not add a second cartoon character.

Extract the bottom background color from the photo or object; use a restrained limited palette and leave about 22%–30% continuous empty space. Avoid sticker walls, dense decoration, and complex scenes.

Generate a short English title from the photo, paired with the label “PHOTO PLAY 01” and one observational English line. Main title: larger hand-lettered type with a retro cartoon feel; supporting text clear and restrained, matching the object's print material.

Overall: an editorial poster where real photography and a retro object-cartoon coexist — light, humorous, smart, stylish — while keeping the emotion of a real travel photo.

Avoid: cartoonizing the person, multiple mascots, existing animation characters, brand logos, sticker clutter, face occlusion, bad hands, cheap templates, garbled text, author name, QR codes, and watermarks.
description: From @Hamburgerai — real photo + personified object companion poster. Prompt translated to English.

title: Ingredient Observation Travel Plate 01
prompt:
Turn each local-cuisine photo I upload into its own premium “Ingredient Observation Travel Plate” editorial poster. Output one image per photo. Do not combine multiple photos, plates, or dishes in one artwork.

The input should clearly feature one complete plate or bowl with at least three separately recognizable components (staple, meat, seafood, egg, vegetables, herbs, nuts, pickles, sauce, or garnish).

Use a 3:4 vertical composition with a clear contrast between original food photography (top) and ingredient-observation drawing (bottom).

Top half (~45%–50%): faithfully keep the original photo — plate/bowl silhouette, ingredient counts, placement, area relationships, real textures, natural light, viewing angle, and original colors. Only slight indie food-magazine / travel-publication grading plus very thin film grain.

Do not replating, replace ingredients, move food, change portions, add garnish, or redraw the photo as illustration. Mild environmental crop for framing is OK if the full plate remains clearly readable.

Use a straight, clean, restrained horizontal boundary between zones; a very narrow warm paper strip is OK. No gradients, feathering, dissolves, or ingredients crossing the boundary.

Bottom half (~50%–55%): warm off-white or ivory natural drawing paper with visible fiber, grain, slight stains, and irregular surface.

Do not redraw the full plate in the same composition. Instead, deconstruct that same dish into a spacious paper observation record:
1. Choose 3–6 real, clearly identifiable components from the photo;
2. Draw one highly simplified but instantly recognizable miniature of the full plate/bowl, centered or slightly low;
3. The mini plate usually spans 28%–40% of the bottom width;
4. Pull selected ingredients out as separate gouache samples, cross-sections, leaves, clusters, sauce swatches, or structure sketches;
5. Vary scale and orientation into a loose, not-fully-symmetric observation around the mini plate;
6. Use thin slightly hesitant black ink lines, arrows, and numbers to map samples back to approximate plate positions;
7. Keep 35%–50% continuous off-white empty paper — do not pack arrows, text, and ingredients.

Bottom materials language (handmade culinary field notebook):
- matte opaque gouache
- restrained black ink contours
- dry brush gaps
- uneven pigment coverage
- visible paper grain
- imperfect hand-painted edges
- subtle pencil construction marks

Forms should be highly simplified yet keep the most recognizable color, silhouette, cut, and grain of each ingredient. Not photoreal copies, not cartoon food icons.

Palette must come from the photo: compress to 4–6 low-to-medium saturation ingredient colors. Background stays off-white, warm gray, or a very light photo-related tint. One warm accent (sauce, yolk, chili, fruit) is OK; avoid neon and high-saturation menu art colors.

Typography must be grounded in photo facts and usually include:
- a 1–3 word English dish title;
- a place + study code, e.g. “THAILAND / PLATE STUDY 01”;
- one 5–12 word English taste/ingredient observation;
- 3–6 short numbered labels, e.g. “01 RICE” “02 EGG” “03 HERBS”.

If an ingredient cannot be reliably identified, do not invent names — use RICE, NOODLES, GREENS, SAUCE, GRILLED ITEM, PICKLED ITEM.

Use narrow handwritten recipe lettering, old recipe type, or soft humanist sans; warm black, deep gray-brown, or a dark from the photo. Slight broken ink, paper tooth, and handmade irregularity are welcome.

Main title must stay readable at chat-preview size; numbers/labels can be smaller but not decorative hairlines. Keep text in one continuous blank area like notes on paper — not slick overlaid digital type.

Overall feel: a traveler tasting a local dish, then carefully taking it apart, observing, and recording it — restrained, warm, clear, handmade, with a touch of taste-memory / travel archive.

Hard avoids: no clear single-plate subject; full multi-dish tables; multi-plate collages; restaurant/chef as hero; invented ingredients; adding ingredients not in the photo; redrawing the full plate to scale; realistic menu illustration; dense nutrition infographics; cartoon food; slick vector icons; plastic 3D food; full-bleed busy backgrounds; excessive text; prices; brands; logos; author name; signature; date; QR; URL; social UI; garbled text; fake Chinese; watermarks.
description: From @Hamburgerai — food plate study poster. Prompt translated to English.
